q: Name a CPU instruction set architecture.

answers.l: From Intel’s 8086, 1978. Every x86 PC still starts up in 16-bit real mode.
Acorn RISC Machine, 1985. The first chip once ran with its power pin disconnected, on leakage from its inputs.
Berkeley, 2010. Open and royalty-free. The V marks the fifth Berkeley RISC design.
AMD’s 64-bit extension, 2000. Intel adopted it after Itanium faltered.
ARM’s 64-bit state. Apple shipped it first, in the 2013 iPhone 5s.
John Hennessy’s Stanford project. Inside the PlayStation, PS2, N64 and countless routers.
Apple, IBM and Motorola, 1991. Macs until 2006, plus the Xbox 360, Wii and PS3.
Sun, 1987. Famous for register windows.
MOS Technology, 1975, sold for $25. Apple II, Commodore 64 and the NES.
Zilog, 1976, founded by Federico Faggin. Still inside TI graphing calculators.
Motorola, 1979. The original Macintosh, the Amiga and the Sega Genesis.
Intel and HP’s EPIC architecture, nicknamed "Itanic."
Atmel’s 8-bit RISC behind the original Arduino.
A stack machine designed to be compiled ahead of time or just in time, not run on silicon.
DEC’s 64-bit RISC, 1992. For a while, the fastest processor around.
HP’s Precision Architecture.
DEC, 1977. So CISC it had an instruction for evaluating polynomials.
Ritchie said C’s ++ did not come from its autoincrement modes: B had it first.
IBM, 1964. One architecture across a whole product line, and the 8-bit byte.
Today’s IBM mainframes still run System/360 code from 1964.
Microchip’s microcontrollers, everywhere since the 1990s.
Intel, 1980. Still inside countless embedded devices.
Hitachi’s RISC. Sega Saturn and Dreamcast.
Sony, Toshiba and IBM. One PowerPC core plus eight SPEs in the PS3.
Intel, 1974. CP/M ran on it.
Intel, 1971. The first commercial microprocessor, built for a Busicom calculator.
TI’s ultra-low-power 16-bit microcontroller.
ARM’s compressed 16-bit instruction encoding.
A stack machine. Some ARM chips ran it in hardware with Jazelle.
Inmos, 1984. Built for parallelism and programmed in occam.
Russian VLIW architecture.
Loongson’s own ISA, 2021.
An open-source RISC that predates RISC-V.
Knuth’s 64-bit RISC for The Art of Computer Programming.
Knuth’s original imaginary computer. Its bytes could be binary or decimal.
Intel, 1972. Designed for a Datapoint terminal.
Motorola, 1974. Its designers left to build the cheaper 6502.
Motorola, 1978. Tandy’s Color Computer and the Vectrex.
AMD’s RISC, big in laser printers.
Intel’s 1989 RISC with VLIW tricks.
Intel’s RISC, in printers and military hardware.
Configurable cores. The ESP32 runs one.
Qualcomm’s DSP architecture.
Analog Devices’ DSP-flavored microcontroller.
Parallax: eight cores called cogs, and no interrupts.
A belt instead of registers. Announced in 2013, still not shipping.
The Game Boy’s CPU core. Z80-like, but not quite.

nope.intel: A company. x86 is the architecture.
nope.amd: A company. x86-64 is the architecture.
nope.apple silicon: A chip family. The ISA is ARM64.
nope.m1: A chip. The ISA is ARM64.
nope.risc: A design philosophy. Name an architecture.
nope.cisc: A design philosophy. Name an architecture.
nope.gpu: Too broad. Name an instruction set.

traps.q: Name the instruction set whose mov instruction alone is Turing complete.
traps.l: Stephen Dolan proved it in 2013. Chris Domas then built a C compiler that emits nothing but mov.
